subject: Verbal Reasoning
passage: Network effects occur when the value of a product or service increases as more people use it. Social media platforms, telecommunication networks, and certain marketplaces exhibit strong network effects: a telephone is far more useful when millions of other people also own telephones than when only a handful do. Economists distinguish between direct network effects, in which the value to a user grows directly with the number of other users on the same platform, and indirect network effects, in which the value to one group of users grows as the number of users in a different, complementary group increases—for example, a ride-hailing app becomes more valuable to riders as more drivers join, and more valuable to drivers as more riders join. Network effects can create winner-take-most dynamics in an industry, since a platform that reaches critical mass first can become difficult for rivals to dislodge, even if a competitor later offers a technically superior product. However, network effects are not infinitely self-reinforcing: many platforms eventually experience congestion effects, in which too many users degrade the quality of the experience for everyone, or fragmentation, in which subgroups of users prefer to interact only with each other, diluting the value of the broader network.
question_text: According to the passage, indirect network effects are best illustrated by which of the following?

options.text: A messaging app that becomes more useful to a user as more of that user's friends join the same app.
A ride-hailing app that becomes more valuable to riders as more drivers join the platform.
A telephone network that becomes more useful as more households acquire telephones.
A social media platform that loses value as unrelated subgroups stop interacting with one another.
A marketplace that becomes congested as too many buyers compete for limited listings.

common_mistakes: confusing direct network effects with indirect network effects

subject: Verbal Reasoning
passage: Circadian rhythms are internal biological processes that follow an approximately 24-hour cycle, regulating functions such as sleep-wake patterns, hormone release, and body temperature. In mammals, the primary circadian clock resides in a region of the brain called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which receives light information directly from the retina and uses this information to synchronize the body's internal clock with the external day-night cycle. While the SCN acts as the master clock, nearly every tissue and organ in the body contains its own peripheral clock, which can be influenced by cues other than light, such as meal timing and physical activity. When peripheral clocks fall out of sync with the central clock in the SCN—as can happen with shift work, jet lag, or irregular eating schedules—researchers have observed disruptions to metabolic processes, including impaired glucose regulation and altered fat storage. This has led some researchers to propose that the timing of food intake, not merely its content, may play a meaningful role in metabolic health, an idea that has given rise to time-restricted eating approaches that confine food consumption to a specific window each day.
question_text: According to the passage, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) differs from peripheral clocks in that the SCN

options.text: is influenced primarily by meal timing rather than light.
is located in every tissue and organ of the body.
synchronizes the body's internal clock using light information from the retina.
is unaffected by shift work or jet lag.
regulates hormone release but not sleep-wake patterns.

common_mistakes: attributing a peripheral-clock trait to the SCN

subject: Verbal Reasoning
passage: Green infrastructure refers to a network of natural and semi-natural features—such as rain gardens, permeable pavements, and urban tree canopies—that municipalities install to manage stormwater and mitigate the effects of urbanization. Traditional stormwater systems rely on underground pipes and drains to funnel rainwater away from developed areas as quickly as possible, a design that becomes increasingly strained as cities expand and impervious surfaces such as roads and rooftops replace absorbent soil and vegetation. During heavy rainfall, these conventional systems can become overwhelmed, leading to flooding and, in cities with combined sewer systems, the discharge of untreated sewage into nearby waterways. Green infrastructure addresses this problem by slowing down and absorbing rainwater closer to where it falls, reducing the volume of water that traditional systems must handle. Proponents note that green infrastructure offers benefits beyond stormwater management, including reduced urban heat, improved air quality, and increased property values in surrounding areas. Critics, however, point out that green infrastructure requires ongoing maintenance—clogged rain gardens or untended tree pits can fail to perform their intended function—and that municipalities have not always budgeted adequately for this upkeep, resulting in installations that look impressive when built but that gradually lose their effectiveness over time.
question_text: According to the passage, conventional stormwater systems become strained primarily because

options.text: they were not designed to handle any rainfall at all.
urbanization replaces absorbent surfaces with impervious ones, increasing the volume of runoff the pipes must manage.
municipalities have stopped investing in underground infrastructure.
green infrastructure diverts water away from traditional systems.
heavy rainfall has become less predictable in recent decades.

common_mistakes: choosing an extreme or unsupported claim rather than the specific cause named in the passage
